title: Power from the back of the chip: what changes for AI processors?
summary: A processor needs a steady voltage at the instant a group of transistors switches. In a densely wired chip, the metal that supplies current competes for space with the wires that carry signals. Moving the supply network to the back of the silicon changes the route electricity takes to reach those transistors. What difference could that make when an AI processor runs an inference? An Intel experiment on a fabricated processor core gives a measured frequency benefit. A separate study of an Arm core design shows how the choice of power rails changes the voltage lost along the way. Together they explain which parts of a chip can gain operating margin, why clock speed alone cannot predict response time, and what an engineer would have to measure to establish energy per inference. The comparison also helps interpret recent process results that combine backside power with changes to the transistors themselves.
author: The Bible of AI

title: What Robots Learn from Watching Human Hands
summary: A person can show a robot where a cup belongs without showing how a gripper should hold it. That gap between a visible goal and an executable action shapes how robots learn from human demonstrations. This review examines six studies of physical manipulation, from learning through practice after a single demonstration to estimating robot actions from synthetic video. Some systems use human motion to guide a controller trained on robot demonstrations. Others recover relations between hands and objects or exploit experience acquired across robots and environments. We examine what each system observes, which information must come from elsewhere, and how researchers measure transfer on physical hardware. Success under a change of viewpoint answers a different question from success after an object slips. These distinctions clarify the contribution of the human demonstrator and show why the strongest evidence for learning comes from tasks that test which features of the demonstration matter.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Who answers for AI? Lessons from the newsroom and the assembly line
summary: A reader wrongly identified in a photograph needs a correction. A driver warned about a faulty weld needs to know whether the car is safe. Neither can get an answer from the machine that helped make the product. A newspaper, a documented vehicle recall and a ruling about an airline’s chatbot show how to trace responsibility to the people and organisations that can act. An AI label can tell us how an image was made. Who will put things right?
author: Juan Antonio Lloret Egea

title: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3
summary: If a language model can rewrite the software it uses to play a game, how can it tell whether an edit was worth keeping? Jens Lehmann and Sahar Vahdati let each model build a program, play five practice games and revise that program twice. They then compared all three versions on twenty games whose results had been withheld during development. Across 27 independent sequences, the practice scores rose by 8.42 points on average. On the reserved games, the gain shrank to 2.80 points, and twelve sequences finished below their starting score. Cost tells a similarly mixed story. Eighteen final programs were cheaper to run, but only nine of those also played better. By preserving the original programs and their descendants, the study reveals something a final leaderboard cannot show on its own: when an agent already plays well, how much of that ability did it acquire through revision, and how much was present from the start?
author: The Bible of AI

title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
summary: Can a research agent tell when its own calculation has led it astray? In FrontierPhysics, physicists turned investigations from their own laboratories and research groups into 56 problems. An agent receives a brief, explores the literature, chooses a method and submits a manuscript alongside results that an examiner can check. The strongest configuration passed 46 of 168 trials. It solved 25 problems at least once in three attempts, but only eight on every attempt. The most revealing findings emerged when physicists revisited the experimental records. Some agents had checked a result using the very assumption that produced it. In other cases, a sound answer had failed the examiner’s test. Nine such judgements changed in the detailed audit of one configuration. Together, the repeated trials and the expert review illuminate a practical question for any physicist considering an agent’s work. What evidence would persuade another researcher that the result survives a genuinely independent check?
author: The Bible of AI

title: Who gets to say yes to AI? A data centre in your town
summary: Who pays for the power lines when a data centre leaves town? Residents weigh promised jobs against electricity demand, water use and the cost of putting things right. U.S. survey evidence shows how public attitudes towards energy costs and the environment have changed. Global electricity projections tell a different part of the story. This opening essay follows the decision back to the town that must live with it, from the promise of permanent jobs to water use in a dry year. It asks what residents should be able to inspect before a permit is granted, how people who seldom attend a public hearing can take part, and which conditions would give them a remedy if a promise is broken.
author: Juan Antonio Lloret Egea

title: Computing where data lives: what resistive memory could change for AI
summary: A neural network uses the same learned weights for many predictions. Keeping those weights in a resistive memory array lets an electrical circuit calculate weighted sums where the values are stored. How much work does this save once inputs, conversions and intermediate results are counted? Four experimental studies provide different parts of the answer. A phase-change memory chip shows how read precision changes throughput. A resistive switching chip demonstrates image classification and identifies the data transfers omitted from its peak efficiency figure. Two studies published in 2026 examine the cost of programming weights and the difficulty of fitting a small vision model to a physical array. Together they explain where a fixed model could benefit, which measurements can be compared and what a system designer would still need to know before estimating energy per prediction or the cost of deployment.
author: The Bible of AI

title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
summary: With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing? T he romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time. Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”. Continue reading...
